claim: Combining rabies-virus tracing, optical clearing (CLARITY), and whole-brain light-sheet imaging, the authors mapped the monosynaptic inputs to midbrain dopamine neurons projecting to different targets in mice.
source: Combining rabies-virus tracing, optical clearing (CLARITY), and whole-brain light-sheet imaging, we mapped the monosynaptic inputs to midbrain dopamine neurons projecting to different targets (different parts of the striatum, cortex, amygdala, etc) in mice.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the methods used and the goal of mapping inputs to dopamine neurons.

claim: Most populations of dopamine neurons receive a similar set of inputs rather than forming strong reciprocal connections with their target areas.
source: We found that most populations of dopamine neurons receive a similar set of inputs rather than forming strong reciprocal connections with their target areas.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study.

claim: A common feature among most populations of dopamine neurons was the existence of dense 'clusters' of inputs within the ventral striatum.
source: A common feature among most populations of dopamine neurons was the existence of dense 'clusters' of inputs within the ventral striatum.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this as a common feature observed in the data.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior striatum receive relatively few inputs from the ventral striatum.
source: However, we found that dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior striatum were outliers, receiving relatively few inputs from the ventral striatum and instead receiving more inputs from the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and zona incerta.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about posterior striatum-projecting dopamine neurons.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior striatum receive more inputs from the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and zona incerta.
source: However, we found that dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior striatum were outliers, receiving relatively few inputs from the ventral striatum and instead receiving more inputs from the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and zona incerta.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about posterior striatum-projecting dopamine neurons.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior striatum constitute a unique class of dopamine neurons regulated by different inputs.
source: These results lay a foundation for understanding the input/output structure of the midbrain dopamine circuit and demonstrate that dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior striatum constitute a unique class of dopamine neurons regulated by different inputs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly concludes this based on the findings.

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons play important roles in various brain functions including motivation, reinforcement learning, and motor control.
source: Midbrain dopamine neurons play important roles in various brain functions including motivation, reinforcement learning, and motor control (Wise, 2004; Redgrave and Gurney, 2006; Ikemoto, 2007; Schultz, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Many dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error (RPE): the discrepancy between predicted and actual reward value.
source: Recording experiments have shown that many dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error (RPE): the discrepancy between predicted and actual reward value (Schultz et al., 1997; Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2012; Cohen et al., 2012; Schultz, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior recording experiments.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that there are at least two types of dopamine neurons, value-coding and salience-coding.
source: However, recent studies have suggested that there are at least two types of dopamine neurons, value-coding and salience-coding (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009), although the extent of physiological diversity remains controversial (Fiorillo, 2013; Fiorillo et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Most dopamine neurons reside in midbrain nuclei called the ventral tegmental area (VTA), the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), and the retrorubral field (RRF).
source: Most dopamine neurons reside in midbrain nuclei called the ventral tegmental area (VTA), the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), and the retrorubral field (RRF).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical fact.

claim: Just ~30,000 dopamine neurons reside in the VTA, SNc, and RRF in the mouse brain.
source: In the mouse brain, just ∼30,000 dopamine neurons reside in these nuclei (Zaborszky and Vadasz, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The collateralization of dopamine neurons is limited compared to other monoamine neuromodulators.
source: However, compared to the other monoamine neuromodulators, the dopamine system is anatomically unique in that the collateralization of dopamine neurons is limited (Moore and Bloom, 1978; Swanson, 1982; Sobel and Corbett, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: A single dopamine neuron tends to target just one brain area.
source: In other words, unlike the other monoaminergic neurons, a single dopamine neuron tends to target just one brain area, raising the possibility that different functional populations can be defined by the region that they target.
evidence: This statement is based on the limited collateralization mentioned and supported by citations.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to different targets have distinct properties.
source: Recent studies have shown that dopamine neurons projecting to different targets have distinct properties (Lammel et al., 2008, 2011, 2012, 2014; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: A population of dopamine neurons in the posterior medial VTA that projects to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in mice is unique with respect to many features including low expression of dopamine transporter (DAT), tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), and the D2 dopamine receptor, narrow spike waveform, high baseline firing and low level of cocaine-induced synaptic plasticity.
source: For instance, a population of dopamine neurons in the posterior medial VTA that projects to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in mice, is unique with respect to many features: low expression of dopamine transporter (DAT), tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), and the D2 dopamine receptor, narrow spike waveform, high baseline firing and low level of cocaine-induced synaptic plasticity (Lammel et al., 2008, 2011, 2012, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dopamine neurons that project to different areas are located at slightly different, but highly overlapping locations in the midbrain.
source: Dopamine neurons that project to different areas are located at slightly different, but highly overlapping locations in the midbrain (Swanson, 1982; Yetnikoff et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: A recent study using a cell-type specific transsynaptic tracing method employing a rabies virus confirmed that many brain areas project directly onto dopamine neurons.
source: A recent study using a cell-type specific transsynaptic tracing method employing a rabies virus confirmed that many of these areas actually project directly onto dopamine neurons (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: VTA dopamine neurons received a distinct set of inputs compared to SNc dopamine neurons.
source: This study also showed that VTA dopamine neurons received a distinct set of inputs compared to SNc dopamine neurons.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from a prior study (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).

claim: The authors classified dopamine neurons according to their projection targets and defined the distribution of monosynaptic inputs of each subpopulation.
source: In the present study, we classified dopamine neurons according to their projection targets and defined the distribution of monosynaptic inputs of each subpopulation.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: The authors compared the inputs of dopamine neurons defined by eight major targets: different parts of the striatum (ventral striatum [VS], dorsal striatum [DS], tail of the striatum [TS]), cortex (mPFC, orbitofrontal cortex [OFC]), central amygdala (Amy), globus pallidus (GP), and lateral habenula (lHb).
source: We compared the inputs of dopamine neurons defined by eight major targets: different parts of the striatum (ventral striatum [VS], dorsal striatum [DS], tail of the striatum [TS]), cortex (mPFC, orbitofrontal cortex [OFC]), central amygdala (Amy), globus pallidus (GP), and lateral habenula (lHb).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: The authors developed a data acquisition and analysis pipeline using a brain clearing method (CLARITY), whole-brain imaging using light-sheet microscopy, and semi-automated software for analysis.
source: To collect and analyze this large data set, we developed a data acquisition and analysis pipeline using a brain clearing method (CLARITY) (Chung and Deisseroth, 2013), whole-brain imaging using light-sheet microscopy (Keller et al., 2010), and semi-automated software for analysis.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology with citations to the techniques used.

claim: Populations of dopamine neurons projecting to most targets receive a similar set of inputs.
source: We found that populations of dopamine neurons projecting to most of these targets receive a similar set of inputs, while dopamine neurons projecting to TS ('tail of the striatum' or 'posterior striatum') are a clear outlier.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to TS are a clear outlier in terms of their inputs.
source: We found that populations of dopamine neurons projecting to most of these targets receive a similar set of inputs, while dopamine neurons projecting to TS ('tail of the striatum' or 'posterior striatum') are a clear outlier.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings.

claim: Classifying dopamine neurons based on their projection target is a viable approach.
source: These results indicate that classifying dopamine neurons based on their projection target is a viable approach, and lay a foundation for studying the mechanisms by which dopamine neurons are regulated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The authors used a retrograde transsynaptic tracing system based on a modified rabies virus (SADΔG-EGFP(EnvA)) to visualize the monosynaptic inputs to dopamine neurons.
source: To visualize the monosynaptic inputs to dopamine neurons, we used a retrograde transsynaptic tracing system based on a modified rabies virus (SADΔG-EGFP(EnvA)) (Wickersham et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology with a citation to the technique.

claim: The rabies virus used is pseudotyped with an avian sarcoma and leukemia virus (ALSV-A) envelope protein (EnvA), so that the initial infection is restricted to cells that express a cognate receptor (TVA) in mammalian brains.
source: This rabies virus is pseudotyped with an avian sarcoma and leukemia virus (ALSV-A) envelope protein (EnvA), so that the initial infection is restricted to cells that express a cognate receptor (TVA) in mammalian brains.
evidence: This is a description of the technical properties of the rabies virus used.

claim: The rabies virus used lacks the gene encoding the rabies virus envelope glycoprotein (RG), which is required for trans-synaptic spread.
source: In addition, this rabies virus lacks the gene encoding the rabies virus envelope glycoprotein (RG), which is required for trans-synaptic spread.
evidence: This is a description of the technical properties of the rabies virus used.

claim: Only monosynaptic (but not poly-synaptic) inputs are trans-synaptically labeled using this rabies virus system.
source: This allows us to restrict trans-synaptic spread to cells that exogenously express RG. In this way, only monosynaptic (but not poly-synaptic) inputs are trans-synaptically labeled.
evidence: This is a description of the technical properties of the rabies virus system.

claim: The authors injected helper viruses (AAV5-FLEX-TVA-mCherry and AAV8-FLEX-RG) into the VTA or SNc of transgenic mice expressing Cre specifically in dopamine neurons (dopamine transporter-Cre, or DAT-Cre) to specifically label the monosynaptic inputs of these dopamine neurons throughout the brain.
source: In our previous work, we used two helper viruses to express TVA and RG under the control of Cre recombinase (AAV5-FLEX-TVA-mCherry and AAV8-FLEX-RG) (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012). We previously injected these helper viruses into the VTA or SNc of transgenic mice expressing Cre specifically in dopamine neurons (dopamine transporter-Cre, or DAT-Cre) (Backman et al., 2006) to specifically label the monosynaptic inputs of these dopamine neurons throughout the brain (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of prior methodology with citations.

claim: The authors injected a helper virus that expresses TVA under the control of Cre recombinase (AAV5-FLEX-TVA) into a dopamine projection site to restrict the initial rabies infection to subpopulations of dopamine neurons defined by their projection sites.
source: In the present study, we sought to restrict the initial rabies infection to subpopulations of dopamine neurons defined by their projection sites. To do this, we injected a helper virus that expresses TVA under the control of Cre recombinase (AAV5-FLEX-TVA) into a dopamine projection site and co-injected a virus bearing blue fluorescent protein (AAV1-CA-BFP) to mark this site.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: Minute TVA expression is sufficient for infection by ALSV-A.
source: Because it has been shown that minute TVA expression is sufficient for infection by ALSV-A (Belanger et al., 1995), we reasoned that DAT-Cre-expressing dopamine neurons in the midbrain which were retrogradely infected by AAV5-FLEX-TVA would express enough TVA for initial rabies infection in a Cre-dependent manner (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Almost all of the GFP-positive neurons (98 ± 1%; n = 600 neurons, n = 3 mice) were also positive for TH after rabies infection.
source: Based on antibody staining, almost all of the GFP-positive neurons were also positive for TH (Figure 1C–F), a marker for dopamine neurons (98 ± 1%; n = 600 neurons, n = 3 mice).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from antibody staining shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: Injecting pseudotyped rabies virus alone resulted in very few infections.
source: Given that injecting pseudotyped rabies virus alone resulted in very few infections (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), these results indicate that the injection of AAV5-FLEX-TVA into a dopamine projection site allowed us to restrict infection of rabies virus to dopamine neurons in a projection specific manner.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The injection of AAV5-FLEX-TVA into a dopamine projection site allowed the authors to restrict infection of rabies virus to dopamine neurons in a projection specific manner.
source: Given that injecting pseudotyped rabies virus alone resulted in very few infections (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), these results indicate that the injection of AAV5-FLEX-TVA into a dopamine projection site allowed us to restrict infection of rabies virus to dopamine neurons in a projection specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: 77 of 89 processed brains (∼87%) were sufficiently clear for visualization of the ventral-most cells after CLARITY processing.
source: 77 of 89 processed brains (∼87%) were sufficiently clear for visualization of the ventral-most cells, and only these brains were used.
evidence: This is a statement of the data quality control results.

claim: The authors imaged each brain from the dorsal and ventral sides and then merged these images to create a continuous 3D image of the brain.
source: We imaged each brain from the dorsal and ventral sides (such that each image was a 'horizontal' optical section), and then merged these images to create a continuous 3D image of the brain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement of the imaging methodology, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The authors applied multiple segmentation algorithms to classify each pixel as 'cell' or 'non-cell'.
source: We applied multiple segmentation algorithms to this data to classify each pixel as 'cell' or 'non-cell' (Figure 2D; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis methodology, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The authors collapsed all neighboring 'cell' pixels in all three dimensions to generate a list of the centroids of the detected cells.
source: Because each cell was present in several images (at different depths), we then collapsed all neighboring 'cell' pixels in all three dimensions to generate a list of the centroids of the detected cells.
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis methodology.

claim: The authors aligned the autofluorescence image captured from each brain to a common 'reference space' and used these transformations to align each set of centroids into this common space.
source: To compare the distribution of cells across brains, we aligned the autofluorescence image captured from each brain to a common 'reference space' and used these transformations to align each set of centroids into this common space (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis methodology.

claim: Dopamine neurons with distinct projection targets reside in different, but overlapping, areas of the midbrain.
source: As previously reported, we found that dopamine neurons with distinct projection targets reside in different, but overlapping, areas of the midbrain (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 3) (Swanson, 1982; Bjorklund and Dunnett, 2007; Lammel et al., 2008; Haber, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in figures and citations to prior work.

claim: The authors observed an overlapping but dorso-laterally shifted distribution of dopamine neurons that project to VS, DS, and TS, in this order.
source: Interestingly, we observed an overlapping but dorso-laterally shifted distribution of dopamine neurons that project to VS, DS, and TS, in this order (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Amy-projecting dopamine neurons were labeled throughout VTA/SNc and also substantially in supramammillary areas (A10rv).
source: In the case of Amy-projecting dopamine neurons, we observed labeling throughout VTA/SNc and also substantial labeling in supramammillary areas (A10rv) (Yetnikoff et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study and a citation.

claim: The distribution of labeled neurons in the VTA/SNc was similar in cases with and without transsynaptic spread (with and without RG, respectively).
source: Furthermore, we found that the distribution of labeled neurons in the VTA/SNc was similar in cases with and without transsynaptic spread (with and without RG, respectively), indicating that transsynaptic spread between primarily infected dopamine neurons and other dopamine neurons did not lead to the nonspecific infection of all dopamine neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The overall distribution of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is different from those of the rest of the dopamine neuron populations.
source: However, we found that TS-projecting dopamine neurons did not show a similar concentration of inputs: these neurons received many fewer inputs from anterior regions (Figure 3A,B) and ventromedial regions (Figure 3C,D). In short, these observations suggested that the overall distribution of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is different from those of the rest of the dopamine neuron populations (whose inputs largely overlapped with one another).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The basal ganglia and hypothalamus provided the majority of inputs to dopamine neurons.
source: Although we found some differences between subpopulations, the overall patterns were surprisingly similar. Among the brain systems, we found that the basal ganglia and hypothalamus provided the majority of inputs to dopamine neurons (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the basal ganglia, the ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens core and shell), DS and ventral pallidum were the largest sources of inputs.
source: In the basal ganglia, the ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens core and shell), DS and ventral pallidum were the largest sources of inputs.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: In hypothalamus, the lateral hypothalamus (LH) (including the parasubthalamic nucleus [PSTh]) contained the largest number of inputs.
source: In hypothalamus, the lateral hypothalamus (LH) (including the parasubthalamic nucleus [PSTh]) contained the largest number of inputs, and the preoptic areas also provided a substantial number.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: In the midbrain, the superior colliculus and dorsal raphe provided inputs to dopamine neurons.
source: In the midbrain, the superior colliculus and dorsal raphe provided inputs as well.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: The ventral striatum is one of the largest sources of inputs to most of the subpopulations, but is a relatively minor source of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
source: In spite of similarities among dopamine populations, several prominent differences emerge upon focusing on TS-projecting dopamine neurons. While the ventral striatum is one of the largest sources of inputs to most of the subpopulations, it is a relatively minor source of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 3A, Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4.

claim: TS-projecting neurons receive an increased proportion of their inputs from the GP, entopeduncular nucleus (EP), PSTh, subthalamic nucleus (STh) and zona incerta (ZI).
source: Instead, TS-projecting neurons receive an increased proportion of their inputs from the GP (Figure 3C, Figure 4), entopeduncular nucleus (EP, Figure 3D, Figure 4), PSTh, subthalamic nucleus (STh) and zona incerta (ZI) (Figure 3E, Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: After correcting for multiple comparisons, nucleus accumbens shell, GP, STh and ZI remained significant (p = 0.00045, 0.0017, 0.00023, and 0.0028, respectively) in 1-way ANOVA among the 20 main input areas.
source: To statistically verify these observations, we first performed a 1-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) among the 20 main input areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). After correcting for multiple comparisons, nucleus accumbens shell, GP, STh and ZI remained significant (p = 0.00045, 0.0017, 0.00023, and 0.0028, respectively; significant after Holm-Sidak corrections for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: These differences in inputs are mainly attributable to the effect of the TS-projecting dopamine population.
source: These differences are mainly attributable to the effect of the TS-projecting dopamine population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: If TS is removed from the analysis, none of the areas retain statistical significance with the exception of the ventromedial hypothalamus (p = 0.0028, 1-way ANOVA).
source: If we remove TS in the analysis, none of these areas retain statistical significance with the exception of the ventromedial hypothalamus (p = 0.0028, 1-way ANOVA), which appears to be a slightly larger source of inputs to VS-projecting dopamine neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In all cases where percentage of inputs differed significantly, the percentage of inputs from TS was significantly larger than the group mean of the remainder of the populations (p < 0.001; t-test).
source: Furthermore, in all of the above cases, the percentage of inputs from TS was significantly larger than the group mean of the remainder of the populations (p < 0.001; t-test).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Many dopamine neurons are embedded in a 'canonical' circuit similar to VS-projecting dopamine neurons, while TS-projecting dopamine neurons have a unique distribution of inputs and therefore form a distinct class of dopamine neurons.
source: These results suggest that many dopamine neurons are embedded in a 'canonical' circuit similar to VS-projecting dopamine neurons (which are known to encode RPE), while TS-projecting dopamine neurons have a unique distribution of inputs and therefore form a distinct class of dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: DS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the neocortex than other populations.
source: For example, DS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the neocortex than other populations (Figure 4), while VS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the olfactory tubercle and other ventromedial structures such as the ventromedial hypothalamus (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: VS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the olfactory tubercle and other ventromedial structures such as the ventromedial hypothalamus.
source: For example, DS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the neocortex than other populations (Figure 4), while VS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the olfactory tubercle and other ventromedial structures such as the ventromedial hypothalamus (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DS-projecting and OFC-projecting dopamine neurons appeared to receive more inputs from the dorsal-most part of the DS.
source: Furthermore, DS-projecting and OFC-projecting dopamine neurons appeared to receive more inputs from the dorsal-most part of the DS (Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All populations received inputs from the dorsal raphe, but lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from nearby areas.
source: In the posterior midbrain, all populations received inputs from the dorsal raphe, but lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from nearby areas (Figure 3H).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from posterior midbrain regions such as the periaqueductal grey and gigantocellular reticular nuclei.
source: In addition, lHb-projecting dopamine neurons received fewer inputs from posterior midbrain regions such as the periaqueductal grey and gigantocellular reticular nuclei (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most pairs of dopamine populations had relatively high correlations (r = 0.85–0.98) in their input patterns.
source: We found that most pairs had relatively high correlations (r = 0.85–0.98).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis of the data.

claim: TS-projecting dopamine neurons had consistently lower correlations than other populations in pair-wise comparisons.
source: Here again, TS-projecting dopamine neurons had consistently lower correlations than other populations (Figure 5A): TS-projecting dopamine neurons were most distinct from VS- and DS-projecting dopamine neurons (r = 0.65 and 0.69, respectively) (Figure 5A), although the similarity was slightly higher compared to non-striatal regions (r = 0.69–0.82).
evidence: This statement is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hierarchical clustering supported the view that TS-projecting dopamine neurons were an outlier among the populations tested.
source: Hierarchical clustering supported this view: TS-projecting dopamine neurons were an outlier among the populations tested (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons are dorso-laterally shifted compared to inputs to other populations of dopamine neurons.
source: We found that, in several coronal planes along the A-P axis, the center of mass of labeled neurons differed between conditions. Interestingly, we observed that the inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons were shifted dorso-laterally compared to the inputs to other subpopulations (Figure 6).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the anterior part of the brain, the dorso-lateral shift of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is caused by the relatively low number of inputs from the ventral striatum.
source: In the anterior part of the brain, this shift is caused by the relatively low number of inputs from the ventral striatum to TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the middle sections of the brain, the dorso-lateral shift of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is caused by an increased number of inputs from GP and EP, as well as a decrease in inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
source: In the middle sections of the brain, the shift is caused by an increased number of inputs from GP (Figure 6B) and EP (Figure 6C), as well as a decrease in inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: In a more posterior section of the brain, the dorso-lateral shift of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons is caused by the large number of inputs from the subthalamic and parasubthalamic nuclei, as well as the lower number of inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
source: Finally, in a more posterior section of the brain, this shift is caused by the large number of inputs from the subthalamic and parasubthalamic nuclei to TS-projecting neurons (Figure 6D), as well as the lower number of inputs from the ventromedial hypothalamus.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The input pattern to TS-projecting dopamine neurons was unique, regardless of the method used for analysis.
source: This suggests that the input pattern to TS-projecting dopamine neurons was unique, regardless of the method used for analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple analyses.

claim: The inputs to subpopulations of dopamine neurons were topographically organized within and across nucleus boundaries.
source: Although the meaning of the shift is not clear, overall, our analysis revealed that the inputs to subpopulations of dopamine neurons were topographically organized within and across nucleus boundaries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis of inputs.

claim: For each of the 'canonical' populations, between 12% and 20% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum whereas only 5% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum for TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
source: For each of the 'canonical' populations, between 12% and 20% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum whereas only 5% of the input neurons were located in the ventral striatum for TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 7D).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The authors observed discrete peaks of high density within the nucleus accumbens that do not correspond to the boundaries of commonly delineated sub-areas of this region (i.e., 'core' or 'shell').
source: Our labeling showed discrete peaks of high density within the nucleus accumbens that do not correspond to the boundaries of commonly delineated sub-areas of this region (i.e., 'core' or 'shell') (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7E-H.

claim: Using precise 3D density plotting, the authors determined the exact number and locations of ventral patches: 5 total, with 3 in the anterior medial ventral shell, 1 in the medial core and 1 in the posterior lateral shell.
source: In the present study, using precise 3D density plotting, we determined the exact number and locations of these patches: 5 total, with 3 in the anterior medial ventral shell, 1 in the medial core and 1 in the posterior lateral shell (Figure 7G,H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7G, 7H, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dense patches of inputs were observed in all cases, with the exception of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
source: We observed these dense patches of inputs in all cases, with the exception of inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons (Figure 7A–C,J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and 7J.

claim: Of the input neurons in the nucleus accumbens, 16–26% were localized to these patches for all of the 'canonical' populations.
source: Of the input neurons in the nucleus accumbens, 16–26% were localized to these patches for all of the 'canonical' populations (Figure 7I).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The few inputs that TS-projecting neurons did receive from the nucleus accumbens were not concentrated in patches.
source: By contrast, the few inputs that TS-projecting neurons did receive from the nucleus accumbens were not concentrated in patches (Figure 7C,I,J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7C, 7I, and 7J.

claim: Neurons in the ventral patches may play a key role in regulation of dopamine neurons, while TS-projecting dopamine neurons may be relatively disconnected from this regulatory system.
source: Thus, whereas neurons in the ventral patches may play a key role in regulation of dopamine neurons, TS-projecting dopamine neurons may be relatively disconnected from this regulatory system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on ventral patches.

claim: Each subpopulation received inputs differentially from different patches.
source: We next compared the distribution of inputs from these patches between different populations of dopamine neurons. We found that each subpopulation received inputs differentially from different patches.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: mPFC-projecting dopamine neurons received a larger ratio of inputs from the most medial patch.
source: For example, mPFC-projecting dopamine neurons received a larger ratio of inputs from the most medial patch, while Amy-projecting dopamine neurons received more of their inputs from the lateral patches (Figure 7J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Amy-projecting dopamine neurons received more of their inputs from the lateral patches.
source: For example, mPFC-projecting dopamine neurons received a larger ratio of inputs from the most medial patch, while Amy-projecting dopamine neurons received more of their inputs from the lateral patches (Figure 7J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The authors did not observe that monosynaptic inputs accumulated in BFP-labeled areas (the projection sites).
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe that monosynaptic inputs accumulated in BFP-labeled areas (Figure 8A–F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8A-F.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference between the number of potential reciprocal inputs to each subpopulation and the average number of inputs in this area among all other subpopulations when comparing by nucleus.
source: First, we compared how many inputs each population receives from the nucleus that it projects to. We found that there was some variability, but that no population received a statistically significantly higher fraction of inputs from the region that it projected to (Figure 8G).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences when using the injection sites instead of the targeted nuclei to quantify reciprocal connections.
source: Because some of our injections were limited to a portion of a region (for example, our injection into the DS only covered the anterior medial DS), we did a further analysis using the injection sites instead of the targeted nuclei to quantify the data. With this analysis, we also found no statistically significant differences (Figure 8H).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Reciprocal monosynaptic connections are not a defining characteristic of inputs to dopamine neurons with differing projection targets.
source: In short, we observed that reciprocal monosynaptic connections are not a defining characteristic of inputs to dopamine neurons with differing projection targets (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reciprocity analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claim: Most dopamine neurons (besides TS-projecting dopamine neurons) have similar inputs regardless of their projection target.
source: Rather, we found that most dopamine neurons (besides TS-projecting dopamine neurons) have similar inputs regardless of their projection target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall data analysis.

claim: Alheid and Heimer proposed that a major organizational principle of the brain is the existence of parallel functional and anatomical macrosystems.
source: Alheid and Heimer proposed that a major organizational principle of the brain is the existence of parallel functional and anatomical macrosystems, each comprised of a cortical area, a cortical input nucleus (such as an area in the striatum), an output nucleus (such as a part of the pallidum), thalamus, and brainstem (Alheid and Heimer, 1988; Zahm, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: In stark contrast to the proposal of parallel macrosystems, the authors found only loose reciprocity between dopamine neurons and their projection targets.
source: In stark contrast to this proposal, we found only loose reciprocity between dopamine neurons and their projection targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Reciprocal connectivity might not be the general mechanism of RPE computation and dopamine functions.
source: In other words, reciprocal connectivity might not be the general mechanism of RPE computation and dopamine functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of reciprocity observed.

claim: Most dopamine neurons are more likely to gather information from a set of common sources and broadcast a common RPE to many brain areas.
source: Our data suggests that neurons in cortex, striatum, pallidum, habenula, or amygdala may not 'entrain' different populations of dopamine neurons. Rather, most dopamine neurons are more likely to gather information from a set of common sources and broadcast a common RPE to many brain areas (Figure 9), while specific populations with different sets of inputs, such as TS-projecting dopamine neurons, might have different functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claim: Specific populations with different sets of inputs, such as TS-projecting dopamine neurons, might have different functions.
source: Our data suggests that neurons in cortex, striatum, pallidum, habenula, or amygdala may not 'entrain' different populations of dopamine neurons. Rather, most dopamine neurons are more likely to gather information from a set of common sources and broadcast a common RPE to many brain areas (Figure 9), while specific populations with different sets of inputs, such as TS-projecting dopamine neurons, might have different functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claim: The ventral striatum was reported to receive a RPE signal from dopamine neurons.
source: Because the ventral striatum was reported to receive a RPE signal from dopamine neurons (Roitman et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2012; Hart et al., 2014), we reasoned that finding the monosynaptic inputs to VS-projecting dopamine neurons would narrow down the list of inputs that are potentially important to RPE computation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Many brain areas have the potential to directly modulate RPE in dopamine neurons.
source: Based on this logic, many brain areas have the potential to directly modulate RPE in dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that many areas provide inputs to VS-projecting dopamine neurons.

claim: The results suggest that dopamine neurons projecting to the anterior vs posterior part of the striatum receive distinct inputs.
source: Our results suggest that dopamine neurons projecting to the anterior vs posterior part of the striatum receive distinct inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: It has been shown that the anterior striatum is important for skill learning and the posterior part is important for skill execution in monkeys.
source: For example, it has been shown that the anterior striatum is important for skill learning and the posterior part is important for skill execution in monkeys (Miyachi et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Kim and Hikosaka showed that the anterior caudate encodes flexible values, whereas the posterior caudate encodes stable values.
source: More recently, Kim and Hikosaka showed that the anterior caudate encodes flexible values, whereas the posterior caudate encodes stable values (Kim and Hikosaka, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests that dopamine neurons projecting to the ventral striatum signal RPE.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that dopamine neurons projecting to the ventral striatum signal RPE (Roitman et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2012; Hart et al., 2014), however, it remains to be clarified whether dopamine neurons projecting to other brain areas send distinct signals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The results raise the possibility that dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum convey a different type of information than RPE.
source: Our results raise the possibility that dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum convey a different type of information than RPE.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the distinct input patterns observed.

claim: One interesting possibility is that dopamine signals in the tail of the striatum lack mechanisms to update the value representation based on the consequences of actions.
source: One interesting possibility is that dopamine signals in the tail of the striatum lack mechanisms to update the value representation based on the consequences of actions, consistent with the idea that the dopamine recipient neurons residing in this part of the striatum store 'stable values' (Kim and Hikosaka, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the distinct input patterns and prior work on stable values.

claim: It is possible that TS-projecting dopamine neurons are related to habitual behavior or one of the other functions besides reward-based learning.
source: Dopamine is involved in different aspects of reward-based learning (e.g., goal-directed vs habit) as well as a wider range of functions besides reward-based learning, including motor and cognitive functions. It is therefore possible that TS-projecting dopamine neurons are related to habitual behavior or one of these other functions, unlike other dopamine neurons that signal RPE.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the distinct input patterns and known functions of dopamine.

claim: The most prominent feature of TS-projecting dopamine neurons is that there are many fewer inputs from the ventral striatum.
source: The most prominent feature of TS-projecting dopamine neurons is that there are many fewer inputs from the ventral striatum (especially from the ventral patches), whereas the ventral striatum is one of the largest sources of inputs to the other dopamine neurons we investigated.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the data analysis.

claim: It has often been assumed that the striatum sends inhibitory 'expectation' signals to dopamine neurons that can 'cancel out' reward values when they are expected.
source: For instance, it has often been assumed that the striatum sends inhibitory 'expectation' signals to dopamine neurons that can 'cancel out' reward values when they are expected (Houk and Adams, 1995; Kobayashi and Okada, 2007; Doya, 2008; Rao, 2010; Khamassi and Humphries, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical models.

claim: The finding that most populations of dopamine neurons received heavy innervation from the ventral striatum suggests that dopamine signals in these target areas are suppressed when reward is expected.
source: Our finding that most populations of dopamine neurons received heavy innervation from the ventral striatum, which might encode 'expectation' or 'state values' in a RPE calculation, suggest that dopamine signals in these target areas are suppressed when reward is expected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and prior models.

claim: The results indicate that TS-projecting dopamine neurons may not be subject to the type of regulation where reward signals are suppressed when reward is expected.
source: On the other hand, our results indicate that TS-projecting dopamine neurons may not be subject to this type of regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of ventral striatum inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.

claim: TS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the STh, PSTh, and ZI.
source: Rather than the ventral striatum, TS-projecting dopamine neurons received more inputs from the STh, PSTh, and ZI.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the data analysis.

claim: STh is known for its role in motor function and is a uniquely glutamatergic structure of the basal ganglia.
source: STh is known for its role in motor function and is a uniquely glutamatergic structure of the basal ganglia (whereas all the other nuclei in basal ganglia are mainly inhibitory).
evidence: This is a statement of known anatomical and functional properties.

claim: STh receives a strong projection from the GP in addition to the cortex.
source: STh receives a strong projection from the GP in addition to the cortex (Canteras et al., 1990; Francois et al., 2004; Kita et al., 2014) and sends projections to other basal ganglia nuclei, such as striatum, GP, EP and SNr (Kita and Kitai, 1987; Degos et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive inputs from STh as well as from areas that tend to be heavily interconnected with STh, such as GP, EP and SNr.
source: Interestingly, TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive inputs from STh as well as from areas that tend to be heavily interconnected with STh, such as GP, EP and SNr.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the data analysis.

claim: Instead of inhibitory inputs from the ventral striatum ('direct pathway'), TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive more glutamatergic inputs from the STh ('hyperdirect pathway'), inhibitory inputs from pallidum ('indirect pathway'), and also inputs from two output nuclei: SNr and EP.
source: These results suggest that, instead of inhibitory inputs from the ventral striatum ('direct pathway'), TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive more glutamatergic inputs from the STh ('hyperdirect pathway'), inhibitory inputs from pallidum ('indirect pathway'), and also inputs from two output nuclei: SNr and EP (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 9.

claim: Cortical information may be transmitted to TS-projecting dopamine neurons through different pathways than other dopamine neurons.
source: Thus, cortical information may be transmitted to TS-projecting dopamine neurons through different pathways than other dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the distinct input patterns observed.

claim: ZI is related to arousal.
source: Finally, ZI, which is related to arousal, and PSTh, which is related to autonomic function, (Goto and Swanson, 2004; Kita et al., 2014), are additional unique pathways from cortex to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PSTh is related to autonomic function.
source: Finally, ZI, which is related to arousal, and PSTh, which is related to autonomic function, (Goto and Swanson, 2004; Kita et al., 2014), are additional unique pathways from cortex to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ZI and PSTh are additional unique pathways from cortex to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
source: Finally, ZI, which is related to arousal, and PSTh, which is related to autonomic function, (Goto and Swanson, 2004; Kita et al., 2014), are additional unique pathways from cortex to TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: There are functional and histological subdivisions of the ventral striatum.
source: Previous studies have shown that there are functional and histological subdivisions of the ventral striatum (Zahm and Brog, 1992; Pennartz et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: To the authors' knowledge, there is no clear structure or function corresponding to the ventral patches that they described.
source: However, to our knowledge, there is no clear structure or function corresponding to the ventral patches that we described.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: In a previous study, the authors found that calbindin, a marker for patches in the DS, partially distinguished the ventral patches from surrounding areas.
source: In a previous study, we found that calbindin, a marker for patches in the DS, partially distinguished the ventral patches from surrounding areas (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ventral patches are dense 'hot spots' for inhibitory inputs to dopamine neurons whereas neurons outside the patches are predominantly indirectly (if at all) connected to dopamine neurons.
source: These patches are, in essence, dense 'hot spots' for inhibitory inputs to dopamine neurons whereas neurons outside the patches are predominantly indirectly (if at all) connected to dopamine neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: One interesting possibility is that the ventral patches are negatively or positively correlated with the observation of 'hedonic hot spots' within the striatum.
source: One interesting possibility is that these ventral patches are negatively or positively correlated with the observation of 'hedonic hot spots' within the striatum.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential relationship between ventral patches and hedonic hot spots.

claim: Hedonic hot spots are so named because the 'hedonic' desire for food was enhanced by the local stimulation of μ-opioid receptors residing in the medial-dorsal part of the anterior ventral striatum but not by the stimulation of neighboring areas.
source: These hot spots are so named because the 'hedonic' desire for food was enhanced by the local stimulation of μ-opioid receptors residing in the medial-dorsal part of the anterior ventral striatum but not by the stimulation of neighboring areas (Castro and Berridge, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Parkinson's disease, dopamine neurons in the SNc are progressively lost as the disease worsens.
source: In Parkinson's disease, dopamine neurons in the SNc are progressively lost as the disease worsens.
evidence: This is a statement of known clinical facts about Parkinson's disease.

claim: There is a prominent loss of dopaminergic axons in the posterior putamen and a corresponding loss of dopamine neurons in the ventrolateral SNc in Parkinson's disease.
source: In particular, there is a prominent loss of dopaminergic axons in the posterior putamen and a corresponding loss of dopamine neurons in the ventrolateral SNc (Kish et al., 1988; Fearnley and Lees, 1991; Frost et al., 1993; Morrish et al., 1995; Damier et al., 1999; Pavese and Brooks, 2009; Redgrave et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum preferentially reside in the lateral part of SNc.
source: Interestingly, dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum preferentially reside in the lateral part of SNc, suggesting that the tail of the striatum in mice may be homologous to the posterior putamen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The tail of the striatum in mice may be homologous to the posterior putamen.
source: Interestingly, dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum preferentially reside in the lateral part of SNc, suggesting that the tail of the striatum in mice may be homologous to the posterior putamen.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the anatomical distribution of dopamine neurons.

claim: One prominent feature of TS-projecting dopamine neurons is relatively strong input from STh.
source: One prominent feature of TS-projecting dopamine neurons is relatively strong input from STh.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the data analysis.

claim: It has been proposed that uncontrolled, excessive excitation may eventually kill dopamine neurons in Parkinson's disease.
source: Although the etiology of Parkinson's disease remains unclear, it has been proposed that uncontrolled, excessive excitation may eventually kill dopamine neurons (Rodriguez et al., 1998; Olanow and Tatton, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The strong monosynaptic excitation from STh could at least partially explain why dopamine neurons that project to the posterior putamen are specifically vulnerable in Parkinson's disease.
source: The strong monosynaptic excitation from STh could at least partially explain why dopamine neurons that project to the posterior putamen are specifically vulnerable.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the input patterns and prior theories about Parkinson's disease.

claim: More and more patients have been receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) as a treatment for Parkinson's disease because of the side effects of systemic L-DOPA administration.
source: Because of the side effects of systemic L-DOPA administration, more and more patients have been receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) as a treatment for Parkinson's disease (Benabid et al., 2009; Chaudhuri and Odin, 2010; Cyron et al., 2010; Deniau et al., 2010; Ponce and Lozano, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Currently, the main targets for DBS are STh, ZI, GPi (also called EP in rodents) and PPTg.
source: Currently, the main targets for DBS are STh, ZI, GPi (also called EP in rodents) and PPTg.
evidence: This is a statement of current clinical practice.

claim: TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive monosynaptic inputs preferentially from all of the main DBS target areas (STh, ZI, GPi/EP, PPTg).
source: Interestingly, our results showed that TS-projecting dopamine neurons receive monosynaptic inputs preferentially from all of these areas.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the data analysis.

claim: Effective DBS sites might reside in presynaptic sites that preferentially target TS-projecting dopamine neurons, rather than common inputs to all the dopamine neurons such as LH.
source: In other words, effective DBS sites might reside in presynaptic sites that preferentially target TS-projecting dopamine neurons, rather than common inputs to all the dopamine neurons such as LH.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the input patterns and DBS targets.

claim: DBS applied to areas that preferentially target TS-projecting dopamine neurons might influence only the circuits relevant to the TS-projecting dopamine system without changing other aspects of dopamine functions, such as learning and reward-seeking behaviors.
source: As a result, DBS applied to these areas might influence only the circuits relevant to the TS-projecting dopamine system (most of which is lost in patients) without changing other aspects of dopamine functions, such as learning and reward-seeking behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the distinct input patterns of TS-projecting dopamine neurons.

claim: If DBS selectively influences TS-projecting dopamine circuits, the list of monosynaptic inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons will be a useful reference for seeking new DBS targets.
source: If this is true, the list of monosynaptic inputs to TS-projecting dopamine neurons will be a useful reference for seeking new DBS targets.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential clinical utility of the findings.

claim: A recent study found that monosynaptic inputs to dopamine neurons in VTA that project to medial and lateral NAc, mPFC and Amy were similar in all the areas they examined, with the exception of inputs from the dorsal raphe and within NAc.
source: One study found that monosynaptic inputs to dopamine neurons in VTA that project to medial and lateral NAc, mPFC and Amy were similar in all the areas they examined, with the exception of inputs from the dorsal raphe and within NAc (Beier et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Another recent study found that monosynaptic inputs to neurons in SNc that project to medial DS and lateral DS were similar with the exception of inputs within DS.
source: Similarly, another study found that monosynaptic inputs to neurons in SNc that project to medial DS and lateral DS were similar with the exception of inputs within DS (Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Neither of the two recent related studies examined TS-projecting dopamine neurons.
source: Although neither of these studies examined TS-projecting dopamine neurons, the results are largely consistent with our finding that monosynaptic input patterns to most dopamine subpopulation are similar, and strengthen our finding that TS-projecting dopamine neurons are relatively unique.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of the related studies.

claim: The results of two recent related studies are largely consistent with the finding that monosynaptic input patterns to most dopamine subpopulation are similar.
source: Although neither of these studies examined TS-projecting dopamine neurons, the results are largely consistent with our finding that monosynaptic input patterns to most dopamine subpopulation are similar, and strengthen our finding that TS-projecting dopamine neurons are relatively unique.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with related studies.

claim: The authors previously observed different patterns of input between VTA and SNc dopamine neurons such as a strong preferential projection from DS to SNc.
source: We previously observed different patterns of input between VTA and SNc dopamine neurons such as a strong preferential projection from DS to SNc (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most populations of projection-specific dopamine neurons are distributed both in VTA and SNc.
source: In the present study, we found that most populations of projection-specific dopamine neurons are distributed both in VTA and SNc.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the data analysis.

claim: The authors injected rabies virus both in VTA and SNc for all eight conditions.
source: We, therefore, injected rabies virus both in VTA and SNc for all eight conditions.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology.

claim: The large difference in inputs between VS-projecting VTA neurons and DS-projecting SNc populations may not be due to the difference in projection targets (VS vs DS), but rather because of the location of their virus injection sites (VTA vs SNc).
source: The large difference in inputs between VS-projecting VTA neurons (Beier et al., 2015) and DS-projecting SNc populations (Lerner et al., 2015) may not be due to the difference in projection targets (VS vs DS), but rather because of the location of their virus injection sites (VTA vs SNc).
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of differences between related studies.

claim: Dopamine axons from both VTA and SNc are mainly unbranched and thus target one structure.
source: In general, dopamine axons from both VTA and SNc are mainly unbranched and thus target one structure (Fallon et al., 1978; Swanson, 1982; Sobel and Corbett, 1984; Febvret et al., 1991; Matsuda et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: There is some disagreement about the extent of collateralization of dopamine axons.
source: However, there is some disagreement about the extent of collateralization of dopamine axons (Yetnikoff et al., 2014); some dopamine neurons may project to multiple brain areas (Fallon and Loughlin, 1982; Loughlin and Fallon, 1984; Takada and Hattori, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Using CLARITY and whole brain imaging with membrane-bound GFP, Lerner et al. found that DS-projecting SNc neurons have negligible collateralization to NAc and no collateralization to other dopamine target areas such as prefrontal cortex or amygdala.
source: Using CLARITY and whole brain imaging with membrane-bound GFP, Lerner et al. found that DS-projecting SNc neurons have negligible collateralization to NAc and no collateralization to other dopamine target areas such as prefrontal cortex or amygdala (Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Using conventional light microscope, Beier et al. found that lateral NAc-projecting dopamine neurons have broad arborizations going to DS, whereas medial NAc-projecting dopamine neurons do not project to the DS.
source: On the other hand, using conventional light microscope, Beier et al. found that lateral NAc-projecting dopamine neurons have broad arborizations going to DS, whereas medial NAc-projecting dopamine neurons do not project to the DS (Beier et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Beier et al. found that neither dopamine groups (lateral NAc-projecting or medial NAc-projecting) collateralize to mPFC or amygdala.
source: They found that neither dopamine groups collateralize to mPFC or amygdala (Beier et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Recent studies show that dopamine neurons projecting to the target areas chosen in the present study consist of largely non-overlapping subpopulations.
source: In spite of some discrepancies between studies, these studies show that dopamine neurons projecting to the target areas which we chose in the present study consist of largely non-overlapping subpopulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the related studies.

claim: The viral tracing method may allow trans-synaptic spread between dopamine neurons, which would make the trans-synaptically labeled populations appear more similar.
source: Our viral tracing method may allow trans-synaptic spread between dopamine neurons, which would make the trans-synaptically labeled populations appear more similar.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential limitation of the method.

claim: The intrinsic connections in VTA/SNc originate mainly from non-dopamine neurons without TH immunoreactivity.
source: However, the intrinsic connections in VTA/SNc originate mainly from non-dopamine neurons without TH immunoreactivity (Bayer and Pickel, 1990; Ferreira et al., 2008; Jhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Related studies overcame the problem of potential trans-synaptic spread by using CAV-Cre in wild type mice or by establishing a technically advanced method using CAV virus combined with Cre and Flp recombinase.
source: With respect to potential trans-synaptic spread, aforementioned studies overcame this problem by using CAV-Cre in wild type mice, sacrificing cell type specificity (Lerner et al., 2015) or by establishing a technically advanced method using CAV virus combined with Cre and Flp recombinase (Beier et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to related studies.

claim: Related studies also found that subpopulations of dopamine neurons had largely similar monosynaptic inputs.
source: Importantly, these studies also found that subpopulations of dopamine neurons had largely similar monosynaptic inputs.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with related studies.

claim: Dopamine neurons that were infected with AAV5-FLEX-TVA at axon terminals provided sufficiently high levels of TVA to allow for subsequent infection with a modified rabies virus.
source: We found that dopamine neurons that were infected with AAV5-FLEX-TVA at axon terminals provided sufficiently high levels of TVA to allow for subsequent infection with a modified rabies virus (i.e., SADΔG(envA)).
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the method validation.

claim: This is a good reminder of the extremely high efficiency of this rabies tracing system and simultaneously reinforces its limitations.
source: This is a good reminder of the extremely high efficiency of this rabies tracing system and simultaneously reinforces its limitations: although some studies have used this system to examine inputs to ubiquitous cell types such as GABA neurons (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012; Weissbourd et al., 2014; Beier et al., 2015), there is substantial risk for this adeno-associated virus (AAV) to infect not only Cre-expressing neurons in the injection site but also Cre-expressing neurons that project to that area, which may result in direct (i.e., non-transsynaptic) infections by the rabies virus.
evidence: This is a discussion of the implications and limitations of the method.

claim: Proper controls are always necessary for tracing using this system, especially because a very small TVA infection could allow for subsequent rabies infection.
source: Proper controls are always necessary for tracing using this system, especially because a very small TVA infection could allow for subsequent rabies infection.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the method's properties.

claim: The acquisition and analysis of whole-brain tracing data has previously been accomplished by physically sectioning the brain at ∼100 μm intervals, imaging each (or every third) slice, manually defining regional boundaries in each section, and counting the number of cells in each region.
source: The acquisition and analysis of whole-brain tracing data has previously been accomplished by physically sectioning the brain at ∼100 μm intervals, imaging each (or every third) slice, manually defining regional boundaries in each section, and counting the number of cells in each region.
evidence: This is a description of prior methods.

claim: The previous process for whole-brain tracing data acquisition and analysis is highly time-consuming and requires the dedicated attention of an expert in brain anatomy.
source: This process is highly time-consuming and requires the dedicated attention of an expert in brain anatomy.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of prior methods.

claim: Several methods have recently been developed with the goal of acquiring an image of the whole mouse brain in an automated fashion.
source: Several methods have recently been developed with the goal of acquiring an image of the whole mouse brain in an automated fashion.
evidence: This is a statement about recent technical developments.

claim: Most strategies for automated whole-brain imaging either employ serial sectioning 2-photon microscopy or optical clearing followed by light-sheet microscopy.
source: In broad terms, most strategies either employ serial sectioning 2-photon microscopy (Ragan et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2014) or optical clearing (Chung and Deisseroth, 2013) followed by light-sheet microscopy (Tomer et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent technical developments.

claim: Serial sectioning 2-photon microscopy has the advantage of using an opaque brain as starting material, meaning that it doesn't require any clearing steps.
source: Serial sectioning 2-photon microscopy has the advantage of using an opaque brain as starting material, meaning that it doesn't require any clearing steps.
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of one method.

claim: Light-sheet imaging of cleared tissues allows for much more rapid image acquisition since there is no time spent physically sectioning the tissue and also because scanning is done with a sheet rather than a line.
source: Light-sheet imaging of cleared tissues, by contrast, allows for much more rapid image acquisition since there is no time spent physically sectioning the tissue and also because scanning is done with a sheet rather than a line.
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of another method.

claim: The increased scan speed of light-sheet imaging allows for the rapid imaging of whole mouse brains with sufficient resolution to image every neuron.
source: This increased scan speed allows for the rapid imaging of whole mouse brains with sufficient resolution to image every neuron.
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of light-sheet imaging.

claim: The authors decided to use light sheet microscopy on cleared brains because they wanted to characterize the distributions of all labeled neurons across brains.
source: Because we wanted to characterize the distributions of all labeled neurons across brains, we decided to use light sheet microscopy on cleared brains.
evidence: This is a statement of the rationale for the method choice.

claim: Among methods to clear brains, a key distinction is between protocols that employ an organic solvent to reduce the internal differences in refractive index within a tissue and those that use an aqueous solution to wash away lipids and thereby reduce total scattering.
source: Among methods to clear brains, a key distinction is between protocols that employ an organic solvent to reduce the internal differences in refractive index within a tissue and those that use an aqueous solution to wash away lipids and thereby reduce total scattering.
evidence: This is a description of different clearing methods.

claim: Methods relying on organic solvents (such as iDISCO) denature native fluorescent proteins and require subsequent antibody staining.
source: Methods relying on organic solvents (such as iDISCO) denature native fluorescent proteins and require subsequent antibody staining (Renier et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior method.

claim: The authors decided to use CLARITY so that some native fluorescence (i.e., GFP and tdTomato) would remain intact.
source: Because we wanted to visualize GFP-labeled neurons, we decided to use CLARITY so that some native fluorescence (i.e., GFP and tdTomato) would remain intact, although we found that CLARITY causes a loss of mCherry and BFP fluorescence.
evidence: This is a statement of the rationale for the method choice.

claim: CLARITY causes a loss of mCherry and BFP fluorescence.
source: Because we wanted to visualize GFP-labeled neurons, we decided to use CLARITY so that some native fluorescence (i.e., GFP and tdTomato) would remain intact, although we found that CLARITY causes a loss of mCherry and BFP fluorescence.
evidence: This is a statement of an observation from the study.

claim: Exposure to organic solvents dramatically alters the size and overall morphology of the brain, while CLARITY leaves it relatively intact.
source: Furthermore, exposure to organic solvents dramatically alters the size and overall morphology of the brain, while CLARITY leaves it relatively intact.
evidence: This is a comparison of the effects of different clearing methods.

claim: The autofluorescence is dimmer in CLARITY-cleared brains compared to iDISCO-cleared brains.
source: Therefore, although the autofluorescence is dimmer in CLARITY-cleared brains (compared to iDISCO-cleared brains), brain structures are easier to identify.
evidence: This is a comparison of the properties of different clearing methods.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum are unique in their monosynaptic inputs, suggesting that they might also be an outlier functionally compared both to dopamine neurons projecting to other parts of the striatum and to those projecting to other brain regions.
source: Third, we found that dopamine neurons projecting to the tail of the striatum are unique in their monosynaptic inputs, suggesting that they might also be an outlier functionally compared both to dopamine neurons projecting to other parts of the striatum and to those projecting to other brain regions (i.e., cortex, GP, amygdala).
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding and its implications.
